In the moderated Q&A (Brookings transcript PDF, https://www.brookings.edu/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/20260206_Transcript_unedited.pdf) he said the policy rate is supporting the labor market and he does not want to see any more weakening there, while inflation is still above target.

In the banking half of the speech she listed nonbank growth, including private credit, among the well-known financial-stability risks.

quote: I remain fairly optimistic that by the end of '26 rates could go down, but I wanted to see proof that we're back on an inflation headed to 2%.
summary: Goolsbee says he is more worried about inflation than unemployment and warns against repeating the 'team transitory' mistake. He agreed with the January and March holds. He is still fairly optimistic rates could fall by end-2026 but says the war throws a wrench into the plans and progress on inflation is needed. Reuters quotes him saying inflation has to be a little ahead of employment as a priority; Bloomberg's headline says he could see circumstances for a hike.
old_note: Inflation named as the greater risk (+1) while he keeps an end-2026 easing hope (-1); torn, chose 0.

speaker: Stephen Miran
occasion: Interview, Bloomberg Television
quote: We should wait for all the information to come in before really changing our outlook
summary: Miran said it is premature to judge how the jump in oil prices will look twelve months out, that an oil shock is traditionally looked through so his outlook for gradual rate cuts is unchanged, and that both inflation and unemployment risks have become more concerning because the oil shock is also a negative demand shock. He confirmed he trimmed his 2026 projection from six cuts to four at the March meeting.
old_note: Keeps his call for gradual cuts five days after dissenting; path trimmed to four cuts but direction unchanged.

speaker: Michael Barr
occasion: 2026 National Community Investment Conference, Phoenix: 'Developing Communities through Public-private Partnerships'
quote: I supported this decision, and it is my view that we may need to keep rates steady for some time as we assess economic conditions.
summary: In a short policy passage inside a community-development speech, Barr said he supported the March hold and that rates may need to stay steady for some time. Inflation is notably above 2 percent; he wants evidence that goods and services inflation is sustainably retreating before considering further cuts, provided the labor market stays stable, and said the Middle East conflict adds risks through oil and gasoline prices.
old_note: Same message as Feb 17: extended hold with a bar for further cuts and inflation named as the problem; the only move contemplated is still a cut, so +1 rather than higher.

speaker: Austan Goolsbee
occasion: PBS NewsHour interview with Geoff Bennett (transcript)
quote: For it to be realistic that rates would come down further this year, we have got to see progress in inflation, I think
summary: Asked whether one cut this year is still realistic, Goolsbee says he does not know and it depends how long the conflict lasts. Stagflationary shocks are the worst case for a central bank because there is no obvious playbook. If inflation, already above target for five years, starts trending up again, the Fed will have to think through its options.
old_note: Cuts made conditional on inflation progress, stagflation framed as two-sided; no explicit tightening lean.

speaker: Stephen Miran
occasion: Conversation at the Digital Asset Summit 2026, New York
quote: I boosted my policy rate by half a percent, not due to oil and Iran, but due to the inflation data that we received
summary: Miran said he raised his end-2026 rate projection by half a point at the March meeting because of disappointing inflation data since December, not because of oil, which puts his projection at about neutral. Bloomberg's video summary says he does not think policy needs to be 'slamming on the gas' but should not hold the economy back.
old_note: A hawkish revision of his own path driven by inflation data, while still wanting policy at neutral (below the current rate). Revision toward tighter from a dovish position, so -1.

speaker: Michael Barr
occasion: Brookings Institution, Washington: 'Brief Remarks on the Economic Outlook and Monetary Policy' (opening remarks before a moderated conversation)
quote: Our current policy stance puts us in a good place to hold steady while we evaluate incoming data, the evolving forecast, and the balance of risks.
summary: Barr said he supported the March hold. After five years of elevated inflation and a rise in near-term expectations, he is particularly concerned that the Middle East energy shock could lift longer-term inflation expectations and said the Fed needs to be especially vigilant; core inflation was likely 3 percent in February. He also noted near-zero job creation leaves the labor market vulnerable, and closed by criticizing recent bank capital, leverage, stress-test and supervision changes as reducing resilience.
old_note: Calls the inflation trajectory 'a key concern right now' and stresses expectations risk from a new price shock, while still describing a hold; labor vulnerability noted but secondary.

speaker: Philip Jefferson
occasion: Global Perspectives Speaker Series, Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas: 'Economic Outlook and Energy Effects'
quote: I am confident that our current policy stance is well positioned to respond to a range of outcomes.
summary: Supported the March hold. Sees downside risk to the labor market and upside risk to inflation, with the energy price jump from the Middle East conflict and tariff uncertainty complicating both sides. Rate is broadly neutral; still speaks of 'additional adjustments' depending on data.
old_note: Two-sided risks named explicitly, stance described as well positioned; no lean.

speaker: Stephen Miran
occasion: Speech 'Prospects for Shrinking the Fed's Balance Sheet', Economic Club of Miami
quote: It is therefore likely that a resumption of balance sheet reduction warrants additional reductions in the federal funds rate relative to baseline projections.
summary: Miran said he would like the balance sheet to shrink further, by roughly $1 trillion to $2 trillion, without returning to scarce reserves, by first lowering reserve demand (easing liquidity rules, destigmatizing the standing repo facility and discount window, and similar steps from a co-authored working paper). He said the preparatory steps would take well over a year, runoff should be slow and through maturities rather than sales, and because runoff is contractionary it would warrant a lower funds rate.
old_note: Wants a smaller balance sheet (tightening) but explicitly paired with a lower funds rate; no call for an immediate cut in this text, so -1 rather than -2.

speaker: Donald Trump
occasion: Cabinet meeting at the White House
quote: Who wouldn't be lowering interest rates right now?
summary: In a long passage on the Fed building renovation and the DOJ suit, Trump said Powell's interest rates are too high, called him 'a moron at the fed', and asked who would not be lowering interest rates right now. He joked Warsh may never get an office in the Fed building.
old_note: Explicit view that rates should be cut now.

speaker: Tom Barkin
occasion: Speech 'Driving Through Economic Fog (Still)' (Richmond Fed posted text)
quote: it felt prudent to hold rates and await more clarity on how we should be leaning to best support the economy going forward
summary: Barkin says the funds rate sits at the higher end of the range of neutral and that holding in March was prudent given risks to both the labor market and inflation and a foggy outlook. Recent PCE data suggest progress on inflation may be at risk of stalling, and that was before the oil price spike; he will watch the shock's effect on inflation and inflation expectations.
old_note: Explicit two-sided risks and hold; inflation worry noted but no lean on direction. Time from the Richmond Fed media advisory.

speaker: Anna Paulson
occasion: Speech at the Macroeconomics and Monetary Policy Conference (San Francisco Fed), 'Monetary Policy and Productivity'
quote: But if inflation is above 2 percent and has been for some time, I would be more cautious.
summary: Paulson laid out low, medium and high productivity scenarios for AI and their implications for the long-run funds rate. She said the 1990s Greenspan-style patience relied on credibility earned with inflation at 2 percent, whereas inflation has now been above target for six years, is 2.8 percent, and the Middle East conflict adds risks to inflation and growth. Faced with a growth surge she would weight the possibility of overheating more heavily; she sees no sign the labor market is adding to inflation. In the Q&A (Reuters, MNI) she said she is worried that repeated supply shocks pass more quickly and durably into inflation expectations, while calling the labor market fragile and stressing risks to both inflation and growth.
old_note: Conditional, hypothetical lean toward caution on inflation but no statement on the next move; between 0 and +1, chose 0. Earlier 'cuts later this year' language is absent.

speaker: Austan Goolsbee
occasion: Chicago magazine Q&A with Mark Bazer (May 2026 issue, posted March 30; interview date not stated)
quote: I’ve been uncomfortable with front-loading too many cuts and counting on inflation going back to 2 percent on its own
summary: Goolsbee says inflation above 2 percent for nearly five years is not something to trifle with and weighs on rate decisions. He remains pretty optimistic rates could keep going down by the end of the year but is uncomfortable front-loading cuts. He warns that an administration ordering the central bank to cut regardless of conditions 'ends in tears', and says he respects Warsh.
old_note: Magazine lead time: text does not mention the Iran war, so it likely predates it. Easing hope and caution offset; torn between -1 and 0, chose 0.

speaker: Stephen Miran
occasion: Interview, CNBC 'Squawk on the Street'
quote: we could be about a point easier, gradually done over the course of a year
summary: Miran said policymakers should disregard the energy price spike unless a wage-price spiral or rising inflation expectations appear, of which he sees no evidence, and that changing the policy rate now would not affect inflation over the next couple of months. He still thinks rates could be about a point lower over a year.
old_note: Explicitly backs about 100 bp of easing over the year and looking through the oil shock.

speaker: Jerome Powell
occasion: Moderated discussion, Harvard University Principles of Economics class (Ec 10b), Cambridge
quote: We feel like our policy's in a good place for us to wait and see how that turns out
summary: Powell told a Harvard class that policy is in a good place to wait and see how the Iran-war energy shock plays out, that there is tension between downside labor-market risk and upside inflation risk, and that longer-term inflation expectations appear well anchored. He said supply shocks are usually looked through but expectations must be monitored carefully because a series of shocks can raise them. Harvard's own write-ups add that he called the deficit path unsustainable and said the Fed is watching private credit closely without seeing a systemic threat.
old_note: Explicit wait-and-see with both risks named; no lean.

speaker: John Williams
occasion: Speech at the Staten Island Economic Development Corporation, 'Ferrying Through the Crosscurrents'
quote: But the current stance of monetary policy is well positioned to balance the risks to our maximum employment and price stability goals.
summary: Williams said the Middle East conflict has pushed up energy prices and could become a large supply shock that raises inflation and dampens activity, on top of tariffs; PCE inflation is around 3 percent. Longer-term expectations remain anchored and there are no second-round tariff effects. He called the stance well positioned to balance risks, raised his 2026 inflation forecast to about 2-3/4 percent, and dropped the earlier language about eventual further reductions. He told reporters that uncertainties and risks to both goals have increased and that he is using energy market pricing as his guide while watching for other scenarios.
old_note: Two-sided risks and 'well positioned'; no easing-bias sentence this time and no tightening lean.

speaker: Tom Barkin
occasion: Reuters interview (conducted Tuesday March 31, published April 1; via SRN News)
quote: The hike case would be around inflation expectations starting to finally move,
summary: Barkin says households and firms still view the oil shock through a short-term lens; spending outside gasoline looks healthy. Scenarios could push the Fed in any direction: a hike would hinge on inflation expectations moving, which he does not see yet, while cuts would need inflation heading quickly to 2 percent or a weakening job market. Goods sellers have little pricing power left, services more.
old_note: Lays out both hike and cut cases and says expectations have not broken out; no lean.
